newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: OPEC plays safe on Iraq, looks to freeze quotas.
newsitem.headline: OPEC plays safe on Iraq, looks to freeze quotas.

text.p: The OPEC cartel stood ready on Thursday to freeze production quotas in a bid to keep oil prices high despite Iraq's likely resumption of exports.
The Organisation of Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) conferred in Vienna as news broke in New York of further progress towards easing a United Nations Gulf War ban on Iraq.
A Security Council sanctions committee on Wednesday formally approved a pricing formula to remove one of the final hurdles to implementing an oil-for-food deal with Iraq.
Iraq's chief OPEC delegate, Osama al-Hiti, told reporters he now expected to resume oil sales within "a matter of weeks".
"If the tanker comes tomorrow we can fill it up", he said.

Baghdad hosted a 1960 meeting that created OPEC but been refused permission to sell oil since it invaded fellow founder member Kuwait in 1990. The U.N. accord would let it sell $2 billion worth of oil to buy food and medicine.

For its part, OPEC is enjoying a bonanza of strong oil prices partly because of delays in implementing the deal since Iraqi President Saddam Hussein sent troops to northern Iraq during Kurdish faction fighting in September.
As oil firms scurried to replenish the West's depleted stocks of winter heating fuel, the benchmark Brent Blend of crude ended Wednesday at almost $22.75 per barrel.
That compares with just $18 when OPEC last met, back in June.
Delegates at the OPEC talks said Saudi Arabia favours a freeze on current quotas, that already include provision for Iraq, at least to the end of June.
Iran's Gholamreza Aqazadeh said he would support a 12-month freeze, although Algeria's Amar Makhloufi said he thought that the consensus was for six months.
Indonesia, OPEC's only Asian member, joined the consensus. Ministers said they may wrap up a deal before Friday.

"OPEC is meeting against a backdrop that can only bring a smile to their lips," said Peter Gignoux, head of the London energy desk at brokers Smith Barney. "Oil is up five dollars. That is in itself an incentive to preserve the status quo."
Prices are strong despite both the prospect that the ban on Iraqi exports will be relaxed and OPEC's own quota violations.
Al-Hiti says only "very minor technicalities" now need to be ironed out before Iraq can export 700,000 to 800,000 barrels daily using up in full the OPEC quota allocation.
The ghost at the OPEC feast was that quota violations have already lifted actual output almost a million barrels per day above its agreed ceiling of 25.03 million, even before Iraq sells any oil.
Venezuela alone is alleged to be busting its mandatory quota by as much as Iraq is likely to sell.
Iran's Aqazadeh aired that matter in a bilateral session on Wednesday with Erwin Arrieta of Venezuela. He said the Venezuelan denied being over quota by a single barrel.
But Saudi Arabia is said by a Gulf source to believe that the market is robust enough to absorb more oil.
Among analysts, Barclays Bank economists note in their latest Commodities Survey that average 1996 prices of $20 per barrel compare with only $16.80 last year.
They forecast that they will ease by maybe $1.0 in 1997, based on the "strong possibility" of revived Iraqi exports and more supply from the North Sea, Asia and Latin America.
